meaning: Training where the labels come from the data itself: hide part of the input and predict it from the rest. Every token of raw text becomes a free training example, so models can learn from trillions of tokens.

BERT's pretraining game: pick 15% of tokens, replace 80% of those with [MASK], 10% with a random token and leave 10% unchanged, then predict the originals from both sides. Strong for understanding tasks; can't generate text naturally.
GPT-style pretraining: predict token t+1 from tokens 1…t, with a loss on every position. The same task is used to generate text, one token at a time, which is why it scales into general assistants.
T5's objective: replace short runs of tokens (15% of tokens, mean span length 3) with sentinel tokens; the decoder writes back only the missing spans.
During training, feed the true previous tokens (not the model's own guesses) and shift the labels by one. With a causal mask, all positions of a sequence are trained in one parallel pass.

e to the power of the mean next-token loss: the number of equally likely choices the model is effectively torn between at each step. 1 is perfect; uniform guessing over V tokens gives V. Only comparable between models with the same tokenizer.

Pretraining on raw text gives a base model that imitates text. Post-training (supervised fine-tuning on instructions, then RLHF or DPO on preferences, or RL with verifiable rewards) turns it into an assistant.

A smooth power-law relationship between loss and model size, data or compute (a straight line on a log-log plot). Kaplan et al. (2020): 10× parameters multiplies loss by about 0.84. Used to predict big runs from small ones.
Training compute in FLOPs ≈ 6 × parameters × training tokens (about 2 FLOPs per weight per token forward, 4 backward). Llama 3 405B on 15.6T tokens: about 3.8 × 10²⁵ FLOPs.
For a fixed compute budget, grow parameters and tokens together (both ∝ √C), about 20 tokens per parameter. Chinchilla (70B, 1.4T tokens) beat Gopher (280B, 300B tokens) on the same budget.
Training a model on far more tokens than compute-optimal so it is smaller and cheaper to serve (about 2N FLOPs per generated token). Llama 3 8B saw over 15T tokens, about 75× the Chinchilla amount.

Skills that seem to appear suddenly past some model size (Wei et al. 2022). Schaeffer et al. (2023) showed many such jumps come from all-or-nothing metrics like exact match; smooth metrics often show steady progress.

Stored keys and values of every past token, reused at each generation step so each new token costs one token's work. Bytes = 2 · layers · kv_heads · head_dim · tokens · batch · bytes per value (Llama 3 8B: 128 KiB per token in bf16).

Generating a token does about 2 FLOPs per weight but must read every weight (and the KV cache) from GPU memory, about 1 FLOP per byte versus a GPU's ~150. Batching many users amortizes the weight reads until the KV cache fills memory.
All query heads share a single key/value head (Shazeer 2019), shrinking the KV cache by the number of heads, with some quality loss.

Query heads are split into groups and each group shares one key/value head (Ainslie et al. 2023). Llama 3 uses 8 K/V heads: a 4× smaller cache than 32 for the 8B model, with quality close to full multi-head attention.
DeepSeek's attention that caches one small compressed latent vector per token and rebuilds per-head keys and values from it. DeepSeek-V2 reported a 93.3% smaller KV cache than their dense 67B model.

An exact attention kernel that tiles Q, K and V into fast on-chip SRAM and uses an online softmax, so the n × n score matrix is never written to GPU main memory. O(n) extra memory and far less memory traffic; versions 2, 3 (H100) and 4 (B200).

Computing a softmax over a row in chunks by keeping a running maximum and running sum, rescaling earlier partial results when a larger value appears. Gives exactly the same answer as the one-shot softmax.

A layer with many expert MLPs and a router that sends each token to only the top-k of them. Total parameters grow while per-token compute stays fixed: Mixtral 8x7B has 46.7B total and 12.9B active per token.
A small linear layer that scores every expert for a token; softmax plus top-k picks which experts run, and the gate weights blend their outputs. Its gradient comes through the gate values.
In an MoE, total parameters (all experts) set the memory needed; active parameters (the experts a token uses plus shared layers) set the compute per token. DeepSeek-V3: 671B total, 37B active.

An auxiliary loss α · E · Σ fᵢ · Pᵢ (share of tokens times mean router probability per expert) that is smallest when experts get equal load. Prevents routing collapse; Switch Transformer used α = 0.01.
The fixed number of tokens an expert processes per batch: capacity factor × tokens · k ÷ experts. Tokens beyond it are dropped and pass through the residual connection unchanged.

DeepSeek-V3's balancing method: a per-expert bias added to router scores only for choosing the top-k, nudged down when the expert is overloaded and up when underloaded. No extra loss term and no dropped tokens.
DeepSeekMoE's design: split experts into many smaller ones and route to more of them (more combinations at the same compute), plus a few shared experts every token always uses for common knowledge.

Ways to run a RoPE model beyond its training length by mapping new positions onto rotation angles it has seen: position interpolation divides all positions, NTK-aware raises the base, YaRN treats each frequency differently and adds an attention temperature. Usually followed by a short fine-tune.
Each token attends only to the previous W tokens, so cost and KV cache per token stay constant. Information still travels W tokens per layer (Mistral 7B: W = 4,096 over 32 layers ≈ 131k span).
The first few tokens soak up spare attention weight in trained LLMs. StreamingLLM keeps 4 of them plus a recent window so sliding-window generation stays stable for millions of tokens.

Exact attention over very long sequences split across GPUs in a ring: each device keeps its query block and passes key/value blocks to its neighbour while computing, overlapping communication with math.
Models use information at the start and end of a long prompt better than in the middle, giving a U-shaped accuracy curve (Liu et al. 2023). Put key material at the edges or retrieve less.

NIAH hides one fact in long filler text and asks for it; most long-context models pass. RULER adds multiple needles, tracing and aggregation, and shows effective context is often far shorter than advertised.
